questions.q: What are CloudWatch's three core pillars of data?
options: Metrics, logs, and events
Buckets, keys, and objects
Shards, streams, and partitions
Clusters, nodes, and queries
questions.explain: CloudWatch organizes observability data into numeric metrics, text logs, and near-real-time events describing state changes.

options: A container that groups related metrics, usually by AWS service
A single log line written by a Lambda function
A folder inside an S3 bucket
The AWS account ID a metric belongs to
questions.explain: Namespaces like AWS/Lambda or AWS/S3 group related metrics together by the service that produced them.

questions.q: What does a dimension like `FunctionName` do for a Lambda `Errors` metric?
options: Isolates the error count for one specific function instead of an undifferentiated total
Deletes the metric after 24 hours
Converts the metric into a log group
Triggers an alarm automatically
questions.explain: Dimensions are name/value pairs that further identify which specific resource a metric describes, letting you filter to one function among many.

options: Log groups (typically one per resource) contain log streams, the individual sequences of log events
All logs from every AWS account share one global log file
Logs are stored only inside the metric namespace, with no separate structure
Each log line is its own separate log group
questions.explain: A log group is the top-level container (like /aws/lambda/my-function), and log streams within it hold the individual sequences of log events.

questions.q: Why does this lesson distinguish 'it ran successfully once' from 'it's monitored'?
options: Because real monitoring means metrics and logs are collected continuously, producing a signal even when nobody is watching
Because CloudWatch only records data during business hours
Because a pipeline only needs monitoring during its first week in production
Because monitoring and logging are the exact same thing
questions.explain: A one-time successful run observed by a human isn't the same as continuous, automated data collection that surfaces failures whether or not anyone is watching in the moment.
